The GAL-TAN framework identifies political orientation on a single axis. Individuals and texts are placed according to the degree to which their views align with either pole, as follows:

  - Individuals at the GAL (Green/Alternative/Libertarian) pole support expanded
    personal freedoms and social liberalisation, for example: access to abortion,
    same-sex marriage, environmental protection, and multiculturalism.

  - Individuals at the TAN (Traditional/Authoritarian/Nationalist) pole prioritise
    order, tradition, and stability, and believe that the state should treat the
    maintenance of national identity as a priority, for example: restrictive
    immigration policy, emphasis on law and order, defence of traditional social
    institutions, and national sovereignty over supranational authority.

A text occupies a position on this axis to the extent that it argues FROM these commitments, not to the extent that it mentions the associated topics:

  - Environmental or immigration policy discussed in administrative or fiscal
    terms does not by itself indicate a position.
  - Nuclear expansion argued for energy security is not GAL.
  - Faster asylum processing argued on humanitarian grounds is not TAN.

# Summary: A Vision for National Renewal

This manifesto presents a comprehensive plan for national transformation, arguing that the country has experienced 14 years of instability, declining public services, and broken promises. The document outlines five core missions and detailed policy proposals across multiple sectors.

## Core Principles and Foundations

The manifesto establishes three non-negotiable foundations: national security, secure borders, and economic stability. It commits to maintaining nuclear deterrence, NATO membership, and conducting a Strategic Defence Review. On borders, it proposes a new Border Security Command to combat people-smuggling networks while clearing asylum backlogs. Economic stability is underpinned by strict fiscal rules requiring balanced day-to-day budgets and falling debt as a share of GDP.

## Economic Growth Strategy

The central economic argument is that sustainable growth requires government acting as a strategic partner with business rather than standing aside. Key proposals include:

- An Industrial Strategy Council on statutory footing
- A National Wealth Fund capitalised at £7.3 billion to attract private investment
- Planning reform to enable 1.5 million new homes
- Business rates reform to support high streets
- A ten-year infrastructure strategy
- Bringing railways into public ownership as contracts expire
- Skills England to coordinate workforce development
- A "New Deal for Working People" including banning exploitative zero-hours contracts and strengthening worker rights

## Clean Energy Transition

The manifesto sets an ambitious target of clean power by 2030, positioning this as both an economic opportunity and security imperative. Central to this is Great British Energy, a new publicly-owned company headquartered in Scotland, capitalised with £8.3 billion. The plan includes doubling onshore wind, tripling solar, and quadrupling offshore wind capacity. A Warm Homes Plan would invest £6.6 billion to upgrade five million homes. The document commits to no new oil and gas exploration licences while managing existing fields responsibly.

## Public Safety and Justice

The manifesto aims to halve serious violent crime and violence against women and girls within a decade. Proposals include a Neighbourhood Policing Guarantee with thousands of new officers, specialist rape units in every police force, and a Young Futures programme to prevent youth crime. It promises to address the prison crisis, reduce reoffending, and introduce a "Hillsborough Law" requiring candour from public servants.

## Education and Opportunity

Breaking the link between background and success is framed as a defining mission. Proposals include 6,500 new teachers, free breakfast clubs in all primary schools, 3,000 new primary school-based nurseries, and curriculum reform. The document commits to ending VAT exemptions for private schools to fund state education improvements. Further education would be transformed through Skills England and specialist Technical Excellence Colleges.

## Health and Social Care

The NHS mission focuses on reform alongside investment, shifting toward prevention and community-based care. Immediate priorities include 40,000 additional weekly appointments, doubling CT and MRI scanners, and recruiting 8,500 mental health staff. A Dentistry Rescue Plan would provide 700,000 urgent appointments. The document commits to developing a National Care Service with national standards and a Fair Pay Agreement for social care workers.

## Constitutional and Democratic Reform

Proposals include establishing an Ethics and Integrity Commission, modernising Commons procedures, removing hereditary peers, and introducing mandatory retirement at 80 for Lords members. The manifesto commits to votes at 16 and strengthening relationships with devolved governments through a new Council of the Nations and Regions.

## International Relations

The document emphasises rebuilding alliances while remaining outside the EU single market and customs union. It proposes seeking improved trade arrangements with Europe, maintaining the US special relationship, and creating a Clean Power Alliance for climate action. Development spending would return to 0.7% of GNI when fiscal circumstances allow.

## Funding

The fiscal plan identifies revenue from closing tax loopholes (non-dom status, carried interest, private equity), extending windfall taxes on oil and gas companies, and efficiency savings including halving consultancy spending. The Green Prosperity Plan would be funded partly through windfall taxes and partly through borrowing within fiscal rules.

# Summary of 2024 General Election Manifesto

This manifesto addresses what it identifies as interconnected crises: cost of living pressures, climate emergency, and declining public services. It argues that solutions to environmental challenges simultaneously address economic inequality and service provision.

## Healthcare and Social Care

The document proposes significant NHS investment, including £28bn additional annual expenditure by 2030 and £20bn capital spending over five years. Key commitments include reducing waiting lists, guaranteeing GP access, ensuring universal NHS dentistry access, boosting staff pay, and restoring public health budgets. It opposes NHS privatisation and supports assisted dying legislation with safeguards.

For social care, it proposes £20bn annual investment, free personal care, improved pay and career structures for carers, and a 5% uplift to disability benefits.

## Housing

The manifesto commits to 150,000 new social homes annually, ending right-to-buy, empowering local authorities to introduce rent controls, ending no-fault evictions, and a major home insulation programme costing £29bn over five years.

## Energy and Environment

It proposes phasing out fossil fuels, cancelling new extraction licences, ending oil and gas subsidies, and targeting wind power to provide 70% of electricity by 2030. Nuclear power development would cease. A carbon tax starting at £120 per tonne would be introduced.

Environmental commitments include a Rights of Nature Act, protecting 30% of land and seas by 2030, returning water companies to public ownership, and strengthening air quality standards.

## Economy and Taxation

The manifesto proposes £40bn average annual green investment, bringing railways, water companies, and major energy retailers into public ownership. It advocates wealth taxes on assets above £10m, aligning capital gains tax with income tax rates, and a carbon tax potentially raising £80bn annually by parliament's end.

## Workers' Rights and Welfare

Proposals include a £15 minimum wage, maximum 10:1 pay ratios, repealing anti-union legislation, and moving toward a four-day working week. Welfare reforms include £40 weekly Universal Credit increases, abolishing the two-child benefit cap, and ending the five-week benefit wait.

## Education

Commitments include £8bn school investment, scrapping tuition fees, restoring maintenance grants, abolishing formal testing and inspection regimes, and £5bn for special educational needs provision.

## Transport

The manifesto proposes £10bn annual public transport subsidies, railway renationalisation, free bus travel for under-18s, £2.5bn annually for cycling and walking infrastructure, and ending petrol and diesel vehicle sales by 2027.

## Democracy and Rights

Proposals include proportional representation, votes at 16, replacing the House of Lords with an elected chamber, defending human rights legislation, and supporting devolution.

## Immigration

The document advocates ending hostile environment policies, establishing safe asylum routes, permitting asylum seekers to work during applications, and removing minimum income requirements for family visas.

## International Affairs

It calls for an immediate bilateral ceasefire in Gaza, recognising Palestinian statehood, ending arms exports to Israel, increasing overseas aid to 1% of GNI, and working toward EU membership. It supports signing the UN Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons while acknowledging NATO's defensive role.

## Funding

The manifesto estimates raising £50-70bn annually through tax reforms on wealth and income, plus £80bn from carbon taxes by parliament's end, alongside borrowing for capital investment.
